fetched_contents.title: Airborne particulate matter from livestock production systems: A review of an air pollution problem - ScienceDirect
fetched_contents.text: Airborne particulate matter from livestock production systems: A review of an air pollution problem Introduction Traditionally, particulate matter (PM) from livestock houses has been regarded as an indoor pollutant causing detrimental effects on animal performance and efficiency (Al Homidan and Robertson, 2003, Donham and Leininger, 1984), and on the health and welfare of farmers (Andersen et al., 2004, Donham et al., 1984). Inhaled particles can penetrate in the deeper respiratory airways, compromising animal's and human's respiratory health, contributing to increased occurrence of chronic cough and/or phlegm, chronic bronchitis, allergic reactions and asthma-like symptoms amongst livestock farmers (Donham, 2000, Radon et al., 2001, Zuskin et al., 1995). Research has revealed that PM aspects are not only important due to air quality issues inside, but also outside livestock houses (Pope et al., 2002). Through the ventilation exhausts, pollutants generated in livestock houses are released to the outside environment (Phillips et al., 1998). Agricultural activities in general and livestock production in particular can emit considerable amounts of PM to the atmosphere (Takai et al., 1998). Although the share of emissions from livestock production only represents 8% of total PM10 emissions, and 4% of total primary PM2.5 emissions, agricultural sources are expected to gain relative importance because emissions from other sources will decline in the future according to current legislation baseline projections (Grimm, 2007, Klimont et al., 2007). In The Netherlands, for instance, the contribution of agriculture to PM emissions is estimated to be approximately 25% (Chardon and van der Hoek, 2002). Inside livestock production, intensive poultry and pig houses are the main sources of PM emissions contributing to about 50% (poultry), and 30% (pigs) of total PM emissions from agriculture in Europe (EMEP-CORINAIR, 2007). Outside livestock houses, besides compromising health and welfare of humans and animals, emitted PM can also threaten the environment (plants and other organisms) causing vegetation stress and ecosystem alteration (Grantz et al., 2003). High concentrations of environmental PM are, furthermore, relevant to climate change issues, such as cloud formation, radiative forcing, and contribute to atmospheric visibility impairment (IPCC, 2005). Emitted PM can be harmful itself and it can carry gases and odors, micro-organisms and their components, and other bioactive components which can be transported away from the source causing respiratory affections to people living in the vicinity of the farms, as well (Bakutis et al., 2004, Cai et al., 2006, Seedorf, 2004). Ammonia (NH3) emitted from livestock houses is also a main precursor for forming secondary inorganic particles in the atmosphere (Erisman and Schaap, 2004). These are the reasons why PM issues have found entrance into national and international regulations and strategies of air pollution and control (Integrated Prevention Pollution and Control, IPPC Directive 1996/61/EC, Council Directive 1999/30/EC, Directive 1996/62/EC and Directive 2008/50/EC), and there is growing pressure to evaluate and control PM emissions from main sources including intensively housed livestock. To protect the environment and to ensure health and welfare of humans and animals in and around livestock houses, the concentrations and emissions of PM within such buildings must be known (Hinz and Linke, 1998b). It is necessary on the one hand, to obtain data on two fundamental particle properties: particle morphology, primarily size, and composition, to understand how PM is formed in livestock houses. This information can be useful to specifically identify and quantify sources of PM (Casuccio et al., 2004). Little is known, however, about these two fundamental particle properties. To better understand the processes and factors which contribute to PM being emitted from livestock houses, on the other hand, it is also necessary to quantify the amount of PM which is emitted. There is still lack, however, of available data which offers reliable and comparable information and emission estimates which can contribute to fulfill this gap of knowledge. The aim of this work is to give an overview of the major problems associated with PM in livestock production systems. This paper critically reviews the state-of-the-art of PM in and from livestock production systems, with emphasis on particle morphology and composition. Current investigations of PM sources, levels (concentrations and emissions), the factors influencing these levels, particle size, and composition, are reviewed. Abatement strategies to reduce PM and its adverse effects are evaluated. Future research and strategies to characterize and control PM from livestock houses are discussed. fetched_contents.text: (PDF) Effectiveness of Multi-Stage Scrubbers in Reducing Emissions of Air Pollutants from Pig Houses Emissions of air pollutants from livestock houses may raise environmental problems and pose hazards to public health. They can be reduced by scrubbers installed at the air outlets of livestock houses. In this study, three multi-stage scrubbers were evaluated in terms of their effectiveness in reducing emissions of airborne dust, total bacteria, ammonia, and CO(2) from pig houses in winter The three multi-stage scrubbers were one double-stage scrubber (acid stage + bio-filter), one double-stage scrubber (acid stage + bio-scrubber), and one triple-stage scrubber (water stage + acid stage + bio-filter). Results showed that these scrubbers reduced concentrations of PM(10) by 61% to 93%, concentrations of PM(2.5) by 47% to 90%, concentrations of airborne total bacteria by 46% to 85%, and concentrations of ammonia by 70% to 100%. Concentrations of CO(2) were not affected. Most of the airborne bacteria emitted from the pig houses were larger than 3.3 mu m (73% to 95%). The multi-stage scrubbers removed 53% to 92% of them, compared with -42% to 20% removal effectiveness of the bacteria in the size range of 0.65 to 3.3,mu m. The triple-stage scrubber was the most efficient in removing dust and ammonia. Compared to single-stage scrubbers, all three multi-stage scrubbers performed more consistently in reduction of PM(10), PM(2.5), total bacteria, and ammonia emissions from livestock houses and removed these pollutants more efficiently. It should be noted that all measurements were performed in winter at low ventilation rates, thus at low loadings of the multi-stage scrubbers. fetched_contents.text: Air scrubbers Background Air scrubbers are an air-purification system that removes particulate matter and/or other gaseous pollutants from the air of a building before being released to the atmosphere. They are used in many industrial facilities to reduce atmospheric pollutant concentrations and can also be used for livestock buildings that are not naturally ventilated. This technology mainly applies to pig and poultry facilities that have forced ventilation, i.e. do not rely on natural ventilation to remove stale air. Most ruminant buildings are naturally ventilated, with fresh air coming in from the sides and out at the ridge via the stack effect. For scrubbers to be effective all the air from the building must be forced through the scrubber and hence naturally ventilated buildings are not suitable for this system. Even for buildings that are force ventilated there is considerable cost associated with collecting all the `stale air' and directing it through a scrubber before release to the atmosphere, (irrespective of whether an air scrubber is part of a newbuild or retrofitted). Hence, they are not often employed in pig and poultry facilities unless government policy requires it. Air scrubbers can be either classed as biological, chemical or a combination of both, depending on the reasons for installation and problem(s) to be addressed. Atmospheric pollutants from agricultural activities such as particulate matter (PM), ammonia (NH), hydrogen sulphide (HS) and volatile organic carbon (VOC) have significant influences upon the atmospheric environment and the health of animals and close residents. They can also pose a risk to the health of the animal themselves and farm staff (Guo et. al., 2022). Common, fast-growing species adapted to high nutrient availability thrive in a nitrogen-rich environment and out-compete species which are more sensitive to ammonia/nitrogen deposition. Ammonia pollution also impacts species composition through soil acidification, direct toxic damage to leaves and by altering the susceptibility of plants to frost, drought and pathogens (including insect pests and invasive species). At its most serious, if changes in species composition and extinctions are large, it may be that remaining vegetation and other species no longer fit the criteria for that habitat type, and certain sensitive and iconic habitats may be lost, Guthrie et.al., (2018). Many protected sites in NI have nitrogen deposition rates that exceed their critical load, (DAERA Draft Ammonia Strategy Consultation). DAERA have a target to reduces ammonia emissions from agriculture by 30% (2030) compared to 2020 levels. Part of their plan is the uptake of verifiable ammonia reduction technology in livestock housing, hence this investigation into air scrubbers. Air scrubbers can be referred to as end of pipe solutions and have been developed mainly with ammonia capture in mild, but in recent times combination scrubbers have been developed, (acid and biological) to enhance removal of not just of ammonia, but other contaminants such as particulate matter and odour, Melse et al., (2009). Ammonia scrubbing technologies are well researched and ready for practical use. However, costs are high and cost reduction options need to be further investigated. The benefits of scrubber applications may be enhanced by development of scrubbers that not only successful remove ammonia but also reduce environmental impact by achieving high odour and particulate matter removal efficiencies, (Melse & Timmerman 2009). By the start of 2009 in the Netherlands there were 880 air scrubbers in operation, mainly at pig houses and mostly chemical scrubbers, (Melse & Timmerman 2009). From a review of the literature on air scrubbers for agricultural buildings, there are a lot more scientific papers available on biological air scrubbers compared to chemical air scrubbers. This might be because chemical scrubbers usually involve using acids, (often sulphuric acid), while biological air scrubbers are a lot more diverse in terms of the materials used and operation of the system. Chemical Air Scrubbers Acid scrubbers are based on the entrapment of ammonia in acid liquid that is recirculated over a packed-bed and the frequent discharge of the resulting ammonium salt, (Melse & Timmerman 2009). They consist of a packed tower that has been filled with an inert or inorganic material. The packing material usually has a large porosity, or void volume and a large specific area. Water is sprayed on top of the packed bed and consequently wetted. Contaminated air is introduced, either horizontally (crosscurrent) or upwards (counter- current), resulting in intensive contact between air and water, and enabling mass transfer from gas to liquid phase. A fraction of the trickling water is continuously recirculated; another fraction is discharged and replaced by fresh water (Melse & Ogink 2005). The pH is controlled, usually at a value below 4, by addition of acid to the recirculation water. This shifts the equation below to the right, i.e. NH4+ in solution. NH3 (gas) + H2O (liquid) NH3 (aqueous) + H2O (liquid) NH4 + (aqueous) + OH- (aqueous) If sulphuric acid is used, ammonium sulphate (NH4)2SO4 solution is produced. The ammonium sulphate concentration is usually controlled at a level of about 150 g/L, which is about 40% of the maximum solubility, otherwise precipitation will start to occur. (In the Netherlands only sulphuric acid is allowed to be used in acid scrubbers, (Melse & Ogink 2005). Removal efficiencies of ammonia can be higher than 90%. Both pH and water discharge rate can be automatically controlled relatively simply with standard equipment. Acid scrubbing can be considered as a stable and reliable measure for NH3 emission reduction, (Melse & Ogink 2005). Multi-stage scrubbers enhance particulate matter (PM) removal by combining multiple stages with complementary mechanisms that progressively reduce the pollutant load. The evidence suggests that scrubbers work by using liquid to collect dust or particulate matter and absorb gases from air, while wet scrubbers specifically remove PM and acid gases from waste gas streams [N1-R4][N1-R5][N2-R3]. The multi-stage scrubber design is useful when multiple pollutants are a concern, and can have one stage for dust, one for ammonia, and one for odors [N2-R5]. This staged approach allows each stage to target different fractions of the incoming air stream rather than handling everything in a single step.

Each stage in a multi-stage scrubber contributes to PM capture by progressively reducing the concentration of particulates and improving mass transfer. The first stage may remove larger or more easily captured particles, while subsequent stages can target finer or more persistent PM, especially because scrubbers can remove 50–99 percent of VOC and PM in air and 90–99 percent of PM in some reports [N4-R5]. The EPA’s wet-scrubber description also notes that the capture mechanisms work simultaneously in one system, which implies that multiple physical and chemical processes—such as impaction, interception, diffusion, and absorption—are active across stages [N2-R2][N1-R2]. In livestock housing, where scrubbers are used on ventilation air exiting livestock housing, this sequential capture is important because the air already carries dust, particulate matter, and gases that need to be collected before release [N3-R1][N4-F2].

Sequential stages improve efficiency over single-stage systems because each stage can optimize for a particular removal mechanism. Venturi scrubbers, for example, excel at removing fine particulate matter, including PM10 and PM2.5, by forcing gas through a constricted chamber at high velocity, creating efficient particle collection [N7-R1]. Packed-bed scrubbers, by contrast, provide efficient removal of acid gases, alcohols, soluble organics, fumes, and odors [N7-R4]. In the livestock-housing context, this means that a multi-stage system can use one stage for high-velocity particle capture and another for chemical or biological gas absorption, while the final stage may dry or polish the air further [N3-R1][N2-R5]. The review evidence further states that multi-stage scrubbers can remove 61–93% of PM10 and 47–90% of PM2.5 in pig houses, and that they performed more consistently than single-stage scrubbers across PM10, PM2.5, total bacteria, and ammonia [N4-F3]. This supports the general principle that stage-specific mechanisms add up to greater overall efficiency.

Operational factors that affect PM removal effectiveness include temperature, relative humidity, and air loading rate. The livestock-specific evidence notes that the first step of the design process includes determining the proper temperature and relative humidity for optimum performance of the livestock scrubber [N5-R4]. This is important because scrubber efficiency can change with airflow conditions: higher humidity may improve droplet formation and contact, while lower humidity may reduce liquid availability and wetting. The same source also mentions that the study used clean exhaust air and focused on heating performance, indicating that loading rate and exhaust-air characteristics matter for real-world scrubber operation [N5-R3]. The general scrubber literature also implies that scrubber performance depends on the interaction of airflow, liquid spray, and contaminant concentration, which is why multi-stage systems are designed to handle different loadings and particle sizes more consistently than single-stage systems [N2-R1][N4-R5]. In livestock housing, the practical constraint is that scrubbers must be matched to the ventilation system and exhaust airflow, because they require all the stale air to pass through the scrubber before release [N4-F4]. That makes operational tuning—especially humidity, temperature, and flow control—critical to PM removal effectiveness.

In livestock housing, the main air quality challenges are particulate matter (PM), ammonia, odors, and biological contaminants, with PM being especially problematic because it can penetrate deeper into the respiratory system and contribute to chronic health effects in both animals and humans [N4-F2]. The review notes that PM from livestock houses has been regarded as an indoor pollutant causing detrimental effects on animal performance and efficiency, and on the health and welfare of farmers, including chronic cough, phlegm, chronic bronchitis, allergic reactions, and asthma-like symptoms [N4-F2]. Outside livestock houses, PM can also be harmful itself and may carry gases, odors, microorganisms, and other bioactive components [N4-F2]. In addition to these health risks, livestock emissions are a major source of PM10 and PM2.5 in agricultural settings, with intensive poultry and pig houses accounting for about 50% and 30% of total PM emissions from agriculture in Europe, respectively [N4-F2]. This makes scrubber application important not just for indoor control, but also for reducing emissions to the outside environment.

Scrubbers fit into housing ventilation and control strategies as end-of-pipe solutions that treat air before it is released to the atmosphere. In livestock buildings, they are used on ventilation air as it exits the housing and use liquid to collect dust, particulate matter, and absorb gases from air [N3-R1][N4-F2]. The livestock-focused review emphasizes that air scrubbers are mainly applied to pig and poultry facilities that have forced ventilation, because naturally ventilated buildings are not suitable for scrubbers since all the stale air must be forced through the scrubber [N4-F4]. This means scrubbers are best used in housing systems with controlled ventilation rather than in naturally ventilated structures. The design also suggests that scrubbers can be part of multi-pollutant control strategies, with one stage for dust, one for ammonia, and one for odors [N2-R5][N4-F4]. This staged approach aligns with ventilation control by addressing the dominant pollutants in sequence.

Practical constraints and trade-offs in livestock applications are substantial. First, scrubbers are not often used unless government policy requires them, because the cost of collecting all the stale air and directing it through the scrubber is considerable, even for newbuild or retrofitted systems [N4-F4]. Second, scrubber performance depends on temperature, relative humidity, and air loading rate, which must be optimized for the specific housing system [N5-R4]. Third, scrubbers are less suitable for naturally ventilated buildings because they require forced air collection, limiting their applicability [N4-F4]. Fourth, while scrubbers can remove 50–99% of VOC and PM in air and 90–99% of PM in some reports, they are not always perfect and can require careful design, maintenance, and monitoring to achieve consistent performance [N4-R5][N4-F3]. Overall, scrubbers matter in livestock housing because they can reduce harmful PM and gases, but their use is constrained by cost, ventilation type, operational conditions, and the need for integrated ventilation and control strategies [N4-F2][N4-F4].

Multi-stage scrubbers enhance airborne bacteria removal by using stage-specific mechanisms that target different particle sizes and capture modes. The evidence shows that airborne bacteria can be captured through the same mechanisms that remove particulate matter, including impaction, interception, diffusion, and absorption by liquid droplets [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. However, the review evidence on pig houses is particularly informative because it found that airborne total bacteria were mostly larger than 3.3 μm, and the multi-stage scrubbers removed 53–92% of them, while the bacteria in the 0.65–3.3 μm size range showed negative to low removal effectiveness (-42% to 20%) [N4-F3]. This suggests that bacteria removal efficiency depends strongly on particle size: larger bacteria are more easily captured, while smaller bacteria may escape more readily or be less efficiently removed by conventional scrubber mechanisms. The same source also reports that scrubbers reduced total bacteria concentrations by 46–85% in pig houses, indicating that multi-stage scrubbers can achieve substantial reductions but not complete elimination [N4-F3].

Stage design changes bacterial removal efficiency by altering the sequence, contact time, and type of scrubber stage. In the pig-house study, three multi-stage scrubbers were evaluated, including double-stage and triple-stage configurations, with the triple-stage scrubber being the most efficient for dust and ammonia [N4-F3]. This implies that sequential stages can improve capture by giving bacteria more opportunities to collide with liquid droplets, be entrained in the liquid phase, or be physically trapped. The general scrubber literature also supports the idea that scrubbers can remove 50–99% of VOC and PM in air and 90–99% of PM in some cases, suggesting that multi-stage scrubbers can outperform single-stage systems by distributing the load across stages and improving contact [N4-R5]. In the livestock context, the review notes that air from livestock houses contains large amounts of pathogenic microorganisms that may infect animals and humans in the vicinity [N4-F2], so staged capture is important for reducing bioaerosol emissions.

Limitations and conditions where bacterial removal may differ from PM removal are important. First, particle size is a key factor: larger bacteria are captured more effectively than smaller ones [N4-F3]. Second, the same scrubber may perform differently for gases versus bacteria: in the pig-house study, concentrations of CO2 were not affected by scrubbers, and ammonia removal varied by stage configuration [N4-F3]. Third, scrubber type matters: acid scrubbers are more effective for ammonia and particulate matter, while biological scrubbers are more effective for odour [N4-F4]. This means that a scrubber designed for PM or ammonia may not be the best choice for maximizing bacterial removal, because bacteria may rely on different capture mechanisms and may be more sensitive to liquid spray dynamics and residence time than gas-phase pollutants [N4-F4][N4-R5]. Overall, multi-stage scrubbers can enhance airborne bacteria removal, but their effectiveness depends on stage sequence, scrubber type, particle size, and the specific air quality challenges in livestock housing [N4-F3][N4-F2][N4-F4].

The evidence shows that Venturi scrubbers excel at removing fine particulate matter, including PM10 and PM2.5, because they force gas through a constricted chamber at high velocity, creating efficient particle collection [N7-R1]. The evidence points to Venturi-style stages for PM, packed-bed stages for gases and soluble organics, and bio-filter or acid stages for ammonia and odors [N7-R1][N7-R4][N4-F4]. For PM, Venturi and packed-bed scrubbers appear especially effective, while for bacteria, the most important factor is particle size and the ability of the liquid spray to collect or entrain the microorganisms [N4-F3][N1-R1]. The pig-house study also suggests that scrubber stage selection can be optimized for the dominant pollutants in livestock housing: a water stage followed by acid and bio-filter stages improved dust and ammonia removal, while the same system also reduced bacteria [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that PM removal is often better served by high-velocity particle capture stages, whereas bacteria removal benefits more from liquid contact and stage-specific bioaerosol capture.

Design differences explain enhanced multi-stage performance by allowing sequential removal, increased contact time, and better load distribution. Multi-stage scrubbers are useful when multiple pollutants are a concern because they can have one stage for dust, one for ammonia, and one for odors [N2-R5]. The pig-house evidence shows that all three multi-stage scrubbers performed more consistently than single-stage scrubbers, removing PM10, PM2.5, total bacteria, and ammonia more efficiently [N4-F3]. The review evidence also indicates that scrubber efficiency depends on temperature, relative humidity, and air loading rate, so design must be tuned to the operating conditions of the housing system [N5-R4]. In addition, scrubber design differences such as Venturi geometry, packed-bed porosity, and liquid spray patterns influence particle and gas capture [N7-R2][N7-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that multi-stage scrubbers enhance performance by combining complementary stages, improving contact efficiency, and distributing the contaminant load so that each stage can specialize in a particular removal task [N2-R5][N4-F3][N7-R1][N7-R4].

Temperature and humidity matter because scrubber efficiency depends on airflow, liquid spray, and contaminant concentration, and scrubbers are not often used unless government policy requires them because collecting all stale air and directing it through the scrubber is costly [N4-F4]. In livestock housing, this means that scrubbers must be matched to the ventilation system and exhaust airflow, and that operational tuning is essential for consistent performance [N5-R4][N4-R5].

## 2) Why multi-stage scrubbers enhance airborne bacteria removal

Multi-stage scrubbers enhance airborne bacteria removal by using stage-specific mechanisms that target different particle sizes and capture modes. The evidence shows that airborne bacteria can be captured through the same mechanisms that remove particulate matter, including impaction, interception, diffusion, and absorption by liquid droplets [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. However, bacteria removal efficiency depends strongly on particle size: in the pig-house study, airborne total bacteria were mostly larger than 3.3 μm, and multi-stage scrubbers removed 53–92% of them, while the bacteria in the 0.65–3.3 μm size range showed negative to low removal effectiveness (-42% to 20%) [N4-F3]. This suggests that larger bacteria are more easily captured, while smaller bacteria may escape more readily or be less efficiently removed by conventional scrubber mechanisms.

Stage design changes bacterial removal efficiency by altering the sequence, contact time, and type of scrubber stage. In the pig-house study, three multi-stage scrubbers were evaluated, including double-stage and triple-stage configurations, with the triple-stage scrubber being the most efficient for dust and ammonia [N4-F3]. This implies that sequential stages can improve capture by giving bacteria more opportunities to collide with liquid droplets, be entrained in the liquid phase, or be physically trapped. The general scrubber literature also supports the idea that multi-stage scrubbers can outperform single-stage systems by distributing the load across stages and improving contact [N4-R5]. In livestock housing, this matters because air from livestock houses contains large amounts of pathogenic microorganisms that may infect animals and humans in the vicinity [N4-F2].

There are important limitations and conditions where bacterial removal may differ from PM removal. First, particle size is a key factor: larger bacteria are captured more effectively than smaller ones [N4-F3]. Second, the same scrubber may perform differently for gases versus bacteria: in the pig-house study, concentrations of CO2 were not affected by scrubbers, and ammonia removal varied by stage configuration [N4-F3]. Third, scrubber type matters: acid scrubbers are more effective for ammonia and particulate matter, while biological scrubbers are more effective for odour [N4-F4]. This means that a scrubber designed for PM or ammonia may not be the best choice for maximizing bacterial removal, because bacteria may rely on different capture mechanisms and may be more sensitive to liquid spray dynamics and residence time than gas-phase pollutants [N4-F4][N4-R5].

## 3) How scrubber design and stage sequence affect removal efficiency

Scrubber type and stage sequence affect removal efficiency by changing the dominant mechanisms, contact time, and pollutant-specific performance. Venturi scrubbers excel at removing fine particulate matter, including PM10 and PM2.5, because they force gas through a constricted chamber at high velocity, creating efficient particle collection [N7-R1]. Packed-bed scrubbers are efficient for acid gases, alcohols, soluble organics, fumes, and odors [N7-R4]. This means that scrubber type matters: Venturi-style stages are better for fine PM, while packed-bed stages are better for gases and soluble organics. In the pig-house study, the triple-stage scrubber (water stage + acid stage + bio-filter) was the most efficient for dust and ammonia, showing how combining different scrubber stages can improve performance for multiple contaminants [N4-F3].

Which scrubber configurations are better for PM versus bacteria? The evidence points to Venturi-style stages for PM, packed-bed stages for gases and soluble organics, and bio-filter or acid stages for ammonia and odors [N7-R1][N7-R4][N4-F4]. For PM, Venturi and packed-bed scrubbers appear especially effective, while for bacteria, the most important factors are particle size and the ability of the liquid spray to collect or entrain the microorganisms [N4-F3][N1-R1]. The pig-house study also suggests that scrubber stage selection can be optimized for the dominant pollutants in livestock housing: a water stage followed by acid and bio-filter stages improved dust and ammonia removal, while the same system also reduced bacteria [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that PM removal is often better served by high-velocity particle capture stages, whereas bacteria removal benefits more from liquid contact and stage-specific bioaerosol capture [N4-F3][N1-R1].

Design differences explain enhanced multi-stage performance by allowing sequential removal, increased contact time, and better load distribution. Multi-stage scrubbers are useful when multiple pollutants are a concern because they can have one stage for dust, one for ammonia, and one for odors [N2-R5]. The pig-house evidence shows that all three multi-stage scrubbers performed more consistently than single-stage scrubbers, removing PM10, PM2.5, total bacteria, and ammonia more efficiently [N4-F3]. The review evidence also indicates that scrubber efficiency depends on temperature, relative humidity, and air loading rate, so design must be tuned to the operating conditions of the housing system [N5-R4]. In addition, scrubber design differences such as Venturi geometry, packed-bed porosity, and liquid spray patterns influence particle and gas capture [N7-R2][N7-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that multi-stage scrubbers enhance performance by combining complementary stages, improving contact efficiency, and distributing the contaminant load so that each stage can specialize in a particular removal task [N2-R5][N4-F3][N7-R1][N7-R4].

## 4) Livestock housing context and why scrubbers matter there

In livestock housing, the main air quality challenges are particulate matter (PM), ammonia, odors, and biological contaminants. The review notes that PM from livestock houses has been regarded as an indoor pollutant causing detrimental effects on animal performance and efficiency, and on the health and welfare of farmers, including chronic cough, phlegm, chronic bronchitis, allergic reactions, and asthma-like symptoms [N4-F2]. Outside livestock houses, PM can also be harmful itself and may carry gases, odors, microorganisms, and other bioactive components [N4-F2]. In addition, livestock emissions are a major source of PM10 and PM2.5 in agricultural settings, with intensive poultry and pig houses accounting for about 50% and 30% of total PM emissions from agriculture in Europe, respectively [N4-F2]. This makes scrubber application important not just for indoor control, but also for reducing emissions to the outside environment.

Scrubbers fit into housing ventilation and control strategies as end-of-pipe solutions that treat air before it is released to the atmosphere. In livestock buildings, they are used on ventilation air as it exits the housing and use liquid to collect dust, particulate matter, and absorb gases from air [N3-R1][N4-F2]. The livestock-focused review emphasizes that air scrubbers are mainly applied to pig and poultry facilities that have forced ventilation, because naturally ventilated buildings are not suitable for scrubbers since all the stale air must be forced through the scrubber [N4-F4]. This means scrubbers are best used in housing systems with controlled ventilation rather than in naturally ventilated structures. The design also suggests that scrubbers can be part of multi-pollutant control strategies, with one stage for dust, one for ammonia, and one for odors [N2-R5][N4-F4]. This staged approach aligns with ventilation control by addressing the dominant pollutants in sequence.

Practical constraints and trade-offs in livestock applications are substantial. First, scrubbers are not often used unless government policy requires them, because the cost of collecting all the stale air and directing it through the scrubber is considerable, even for newbuild or retrofitted systems [N4-F4]. Second, scrubber performance depends on temperature, relative humidity, and air loading rate, which must be optimized for the specific housing system [N5-R4]. Third, scrubbers are less suitable for naturally ventilated buildings because they require forced air collection, limiting their applicability [N4-F4]. Fourth, while scrubbers can remove 50–99% of VOC and PM in air and 90–99% of PM in some cases, they are not always perfect and can require careful design, maintenance, and monitoring to achieve consistent performance [N4-R5][N4-F3]. Overall, scrubbers matter in livestock housing because they can reduce harmful PM and gases, but their use is constrained by cost, ventilation type, operational conditions, and the need for integrated ventilation and control strategies [N4-F2][N4-F4].

## Conclusion

Multi-stage scrubbers enhance removal efficiency in livestock housing by combining multiple stages with complementary mechanisms, stage-specific removal tasks, and design optimization. For particulate matter, they improve efficiency by progressively capturing larger and finer particles, using Venturi-style high-velocity capture and packed-bed absorption, and distributing the load across stages [N7-R1][N7-R4][N4-R5]. For airborne bacteria, they enhance removal by targeting different particle sizes and capture modes, with larger bacteria being captured more effectively than smaller ones, and stage sequence improving contact time and entrainment [N4-F3][N1-R1]. Scrubber design and stage sequence matter because Venturi stages are better for PM, packed-bed stages are better for gases and soluble organics, and bio-filter or acid stages are better for ammonia and odors [N7-R1][N7-R4][N4-F4]. In livestock housing, scrubbers are important because they address PM, ammonia, odors, and biological contaminants, but their use is constrained by cost, forced ventilation, temperature, humidity, and air loading rate [N4-F2][N4-F4][N5-R4]. Overall, multi-stage scrubbers provide a more consistent and efficient way to clean livestock exhaust air than single-stage systems, especially when multiple pollutants are present [N2-R5][N4-F3].

The review notes that PM from livestock houses has been regarded as an indoor pollutant causing detrimental effects on animal performance and efficiency, and on the health and welfare of farmers, including chronic cough, phlegm, chronic bronchitis, allergic reactions, and asthma-like symptoms [N4-F2]. Outside livestock houses, PM can also be harmful itself and may carry gases, odors, microorganisms, and other bioactive components [N4-F2]. In addition to these health risks, livestock emissions are a major source of PM10 and PM2.5 in agricultural settings, with intensive poultry and pig houses accounting for about 50% and 30% of total PM emissions from agriculture in Europe, respectively [N4-F2]. This makes scrubber application important not just for indoor control, but also for reducing emissions to the outside environment.

Scrubbers fit into housing ventilation and control strategies as end-of-pipe solutions that treat air before it is released to the atmosphere. In livestock buildings, they are used on ventilation air as it exits the housing and use liquid to collect dust, particulate matter, and absorb gases from air [N3-R1][N4-F2]. The livestock-focused review emphasizes that air scrubbers are mainly applied to pig and poultry facilities that have forced ventilation, because naturally ventilated buildings are not suitable for scrubbers since all the stale air must be forced through the scrubber [N4-F4]. This means scrubbers are best used in housing systems with controlled ventilation rather than in naturally ventilated structures. The design also suggests that scrubbers can be part of multi-pollutant control strategies, with one stage for dust, one for ammonia, and one for odors [N2-R5][N4-F4]. This staged approach aligns with ventilation control by addressing the dominant pollutants in sequence.

Practical constraints and trade-offs in livestock applications are substantial. First, scrubbers are not often used unless government policy requires them, because the cost of collecting all the stale air and directing it through the scrubber is considerable, even for newbuild or retrofitted systems [N4-F4]. Second, scrubber performance depends on temperature, relative humidity, and air loading rate, which must be optimized for the specific housing system [N5-R4]. Third, scrubbers are less suitable for naturally ventilated buildings because they require forced air collection, limiting their applicability [N4-F4]. Fourth, while scrubbers can remove 50–99% of VOC and PM in air and 90–99% of PM in some reports, they are not always perfect and can require careful design, maintenance, and monitoring to achieve consistent performance [N4-R5][N4-F3]. Overall, scrubbers matter in livestock housing because they can reduce harmful PM and gases, but their use is constrained by cost, ventilation type, operational conditions, and the need for integrated ventilation and control strategies [N4-F2][N4-F4].

Multi-stage scrubbers enhance airborne bacteria removal by using stage-specific mechanisms that target different particle sizes and capture modes. The evidence shows that airborne bacteria can be captured through the same mechanisms that remove particulate matter, including impaction, interception, diffusion, and absorption by liquid droplets [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. However, the review evidence on pig houses is particularly informative because it found that airborne total bacteria were mostly larger than 3.3 μm, and the multi-stage scrubbers removed 53–92% of them, while the bacteria in the 0.65–3.3 μm size range showed negative to low removal effectiveness (-42% to 20%) [N4-F3]. This suggests that bacteria removal efficiency depends strongly on particle size: larger bacteria are more easily captured, while smaller bacteria may escape more readily or be less efficiently removed by conventional scrubber mechanisms. The same source also reports that scrubbers reduced total bacteria concentrations by 46–85% in pig houses, indicating that multi-stage scrubbers can achieve substantial reductions but not complete elimination [N4-F3].

Stage design changes bacterial removal efficiency by altering the sequence, contact time, and type of scrubber stage. In the pig-house study, three multi-stage scrubbers were evaluated, including double-stage and triple-stage configurations, with the triple-stage scrubber being the most efficient for dust and ammonia [N4-F3]. This implies that sequential stages can improve capture by giving bacteria more opportunities to collide with liquid droplets, be entrained in the liquid phase, or be physically trapped. The general scrubber literature also supports the idea that scrubbers can remove 50–99% of VOC and PM in air and 90–99% of PM in some cases, suggesting that multi-stage scrubbers can outperform single-stage systems by distributing the load across stages and improving contact [N4-R5]. In the livestock context, the review notes that air from livestock houses contains large amounts of pathogenic microorganisms that may infect animals and humans in the vicinity [N4-F2], so staged capture is important for reducing bioaerosol emissions.

Limitations and conditions where bacterial removal may differ from PM removal are important. First, particle size is a key factor: larger bacteria are captured more effectively than smaller ones [N4-F3]. Second, the same scrubber may perform differently for gases versus bacteria: in the pig-house study, concentrations of CO2 were not affected by scrubbers, and ammonia removal varied by stage configuration [N4-F3]. Third, scrubber type matters: acid scrubbers are more effective for ammonia and particulate matter, while biological scrubbers are more effective for odour [N4-F4]. This means that a scrubber designed for PM or ammonia may not be the best choice for maximizing bacterial removal, because bacteria may rely on different capture mechanisms and may be more sensitive to liquid spray dynamics and residence time than gas-phase pollutants [N4-F4][N4-R5]. Overall, multi-stage scrubbers can enhance airborne bacteria removal, but their effectiveness depends on stage sequence, scrubber type, particle size, and the specific air quality challenges in livestock housing [N4-F3][N4-F2][N4-F4].

The evidence shows that Venturi scrubbers excel at removing fine particulate matter, including PM10 and PM2.5, because they force gas through a constricted chamber at high velocity, creating efficient particle collection [N7-R1]. Packed-bed scrubbers, by contrast, are described as efficient for acid gases, alcohols, soluble organics, fumes, and odors [N7-R4]. This means that scrubber type matters: Venturi-style stages are better for fine PM, while packed-bed stages are better for gases and soluble organics. In the pig-house study, the triple-stage scrubber (water stage + acid stage + bio-filter) was the most efficient for dust and ammonia, showing how combining different scrubber stages can improve performance for multiple contaminants [N4-F3]. Similarly, the study found that multi-stage scrubbers removed 61–93% of PM10 and 47–90% of PM2.5, while also reducing total bacteria and ammonia, indicating that stage sequence can improve consistency across different pollutant classes [N4-F3].

Operational factors that affect PM removal effectiveness include temperature, relative humidity, and air loading rate. In livestock housing, the practical constraint is that scrubbers must be matched to the ventilation system and exhaust airflow, because they require all the stale air to pass through the scrubber before release [N4-F4]. The review notes that PM from livestock houses has been regarded as an indoor pollutant causing detrimental effects on animal performance and efficiency, and on the health and welfare of farmers, including chronic cough, phlegm, chronic bronchitis, allergic reactions, and asthma-like symptoms [N4-F2]. Outside livestock houses, PM can also be harmful itself and may carry gases, odors, microorganisms, and other bioactive components [N4-F2]. In addition, livestock emissions are a major source of PM10 and PM2.5 in agricultural settings, with intensive poultry and pig houses accounting for about 50% and 30% of total PM emissions from agriculture in Europe, respectively [N4-F2]. This makes scrubber application important not just for indoor control, but also for reducing emissions to the outside environment.

Scrubbers fit into housing ventilation and control strategies as end-of-pipe solutions that treat air before it is released to the atmosphere. In livestock buildings, they are used on ventilation air as it exits the housing and use liquid to collect dust, particulate matter, and absorb gases from air [N3-R1][N4-F2]. The livestock-focused review emphasizes that air scrubbers are mainly applied to pig and poultry facilities that have forced ventilation, because naturally ventilated buildings are not suitable for scrubbers since all the stale air must be forced through the scrubber [N4-F4]. This means scrubbers are best used in housing systems with controlled ventilation rather than in naturally ventilated structures. The design also suggests that scrubbers can be part of multi-pollutant control strategies, with one stage for dust, one for ammonia, and one for odors [N2-R5][N4-F4]. This staged approach aligns with ventilation control by addressing the dominant pollutants in sequence.

Practical constraints and trade-offs in livestock applications are substantial. First, scrubbers are not often used unless government policy requires them, because the cost of collecting all the stale air and directing it through the scrubber is considerable, even for newbuild or retrofitted systems [N4-F4]. Second, scrubber performance depends on temperature, relative humidity, and air loading rate, which must be optimized for the specific housing system [N5-R4]. Third, scrubbers are less suitable for naturally ventilated buildings because they require forced air collection, limiting their applicability [N4-F4]. Fourth, while scrubbers can remove 50–99% of VOC and PM in air and 90–99% of PM in some cases, they are not always perfect and can require careful design, maintenance, and monitoring to achieve consistent performance [N4-R5][N4-F3]. Overall, scrubbers matter in livestock housing because they can reduce harmful PM and gases, but their use is constrained by cost, ventilation type, operational conditions, and the need for integrated ventilation and control strategies [N4-F2][N4-F4].

## Conclusion

Multi-stage scrubbers enhance removal efficiency in livestock housing by combining multiple stages with complementary mechanisms, stage-specific removal tasks, and design optimization. For particulate matter, they improve efficiency by progressively capturing larger and finer particles, using Venturi-style high-velocity capture and packed-bed absorption, and distributing the load across stages [N7-R1][N7-R4][N4-R5]. For airborne bacteria, they enhance removal by targeting different particle sizes and capture modes, with larger bacteria being captured more effectively than smaller ones, and stage sequence improving contact time and entrainment [N4-F3][N1-R1]. Scrubber design and stage sequence matter because Venturi stages are better for PM, packed-bed stages are better for gases and soluble organics, and bio-filter or acid stages are better for ammonia and odors [N7-R1][N7-R4][N4-F4]. In livestock housing, scrubbers are important because they address PM, ammonia, odors, and biological contaminants, but their use is constrained by cost, forced ventilation, temperature, humidity, and air loading rate [N4-F2][N4-F4][N5-R4]. Overall, multi-stage scrubbers provide a more consistent and efficient way to clean livestock exhaust air than single-stage systems, especially when multiple pollutants are present [N2-R5][N4-F3].
